messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 35

He arrives to sessions precisely on time, often a few minutes early, sitting in the same chair by the window. He is tall, with a quiet intensity, his hands rarely still—tapping his knee, adjusting his watch, straightening the edge of his notebook. He is a tax inspector, and he speaks about his work with a dry precision that mirrors his demeanor: numbers, deadlines, irregularities. It took three sessions before he mentioned the accident at all.

The event happened eighteen months ago, on a clear Tuesday morning. He was driving to a client’s office, an audit that had been rescheduled twice. The other driver ran a red light at an intersection he had passed a hundred times. He remembers the sound—a deep, metallic crush—and the way the steering wheel slammed into his chest. He was trapped for nearly twenty minutes before the fire department cut him free. No one died. He had three fractured ribs, a punctured lung, and a deep gash on his forehead. He was in the hospital for ten days.

At first, he tells me, he thought he was fine. He went back to work after six weeks, eager to reclaim his routine. But routine no longer fit. The first time he sat behind the wheel again, his hands shook so badly he had to pull over. His supervisor allowed him to work remotely, reviewing documents from home. He welcomed the excuse—it meant he could avoid the highway, the intersections, the sound of brakes. But avoidance bled into other parts of his life. He stopped meeting friends for coffee. He stopped going to the grocery store. He stopped driving altogether, relying on delivery services and a neighbor for errands.

He does not describe these changes with distress. He describes them as logical reactions to an unsafe world. When I ask about the divorce, which happened six months before the accident, he shrugs. "That was a different collapse." But I notice he speaks about his ex-wife in the present tense, as though she is still a looming presence. He was the one who ended it, he says, because he could not give her what she needed. He does not say what that was.

In our sessions, he often returns to the intersection. He can still feel the impact in his ribs, even though they healed. He wakes up at 3:17 a.m. almost every night—he knows the time because he checks his phone, then cannot fall back asleep. During the day, he is easily startled: a car horn outside his apartment sends his heart racing; a sudden knock on his office door makes him flinch. He has stopped riding in taxis or ride-shares because the feel of acceleration makes him nauseous.

His work has become a refuge, but also a cage. He audits small businesses now, never traveling to their sites. He scrutinizes receipts, bank statements, payroll records—anything that can be contained in a spreadsheet. He tells me he feels safest when he is alone in his apartment with his laptop and a cup of black tea. He has lost eight pounds in the last three months because he forgets to eat.

He does not believe he has PTSD. "I just have a bad memory and a careful lifestyle," he says. But he also admits that he no longer trusts his body, no longer trusts other drivers, no longer trusts that the world is predictable. When I ask if he has considered driving again, he shakes his head slowly. "There is no reason to," he says. "Everything I need is here." He gestures around my office, but his gaze is fixed somewhere else—on the intersection, on the sound, on the moment before the metal began to scream.
